articles.title: People who favor science over religious dogma are surprisingly open to believing in ghosts and magic
articles.summary: As traditional religious affiliations decline, supernatural beliefs are not vanishing. A new survey reveals that people who favor secular reasoning over religious authority often hold magical or superstitious beliefs, provided they maintain some residual connection to spirituality.

articles.title: Expecting entitlement, researchers asked young men about sex. What they found was fear, vigilance, and shame.
articles.summary: Some young men may have absorbed a cultural suspicion of men so deeply that they see themselves as potential perpetrators, according to an interview study that found fear and shame crowding out pleasure in their accounts of sex.

articles.title: Six future Trump officials wrote books before taking office. All six leaned hardest on the same metaphor.
articles.summary: Before joining the second Trump administration, J. D. Vance, Marco Rubio, Pete Hegseth, and three other future officials wrote books that framed politics largely through metaphors of war, decline, disease, and betrayal. Metaphors of threat outnumbered metaphors of renewal by about nine to one.

articles.summary: arXiv:2610.37732v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many uses of language models end in a typed decision: a choice among a closed set of options, whose probabilities code can act on. articles.title: Scientists discover why chronic back pain feels so personal
articles.summary: A surprising discovery at UC San Diego suggests that chronic lower back pain may become deeply embedded in the brain's sense of personal identity. Researchers found that movement-triggered pain activates a brain network associated with self-awareness and memories, even though ordinary acute pain typically shuts this network down. This unexpected difference could explain why conventional pain medications often provide limited relief and why fear, anticipation, and past experiences can intensify chronic pain.

articles.title: Social media use ranks among the top predictors of depression in a study of 183,000 adults
articles.summary: Most research on social media and depression has focused on teenagers. A new analysis of more than 183,000 American adults suggests the link extends across the adult lifespan and has held steady for over a decade.

articles.title: People in interracial relationships tend to be more politically liberal, study finds
articles.summary: Americans in interracial relationships had 37% greater odds of leaning liberal than those with same-race partners. The pattern was stronger for women and weaker for married, Asian, and Hispanic participants.
